name: Adam Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager on the Ellery estate, six hundred hectares of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, and I farm forty hectares of my own that my grandad left me. This time of year it's drilling the last of the winter wheat and checking the rape for flea beetle. Most of my day is in the tractor cab or the office, and the tractor mostly steers itself with GPS, so I'm on my tablet planning the next job while it drives. Evenings I'm usually at the young farmers' club or round at my girlfriend Freya's parents for dinner.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every single day. I use it to plan seed rates, check the spray rules, read the weather models and write the reports for the estate. I've got a drone that maps the fields and the software tells me where to put more or less fertiliser. I was the first in the district to do that and now half of them have copied me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what's the hard part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love a good harvest, a combine full and the grain dryer humming. And I love the puzzle of it, getting more from the same ground. The hard part is the paperwork from government and the grain price, which is set somewhere in Chicago by people who've never seen my fields.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? I'd honestly be a bit disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and the farmers who use it well will still get ahead. I'd tell people at the club not to throw it out just because the hype faded. I'd post a few things in the arable forum about what's actually worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit let down, because I'd planned on fully self-driving tractors within a few years. But I'd still be ahead of most people. And honestly, a quieter world suits a lot of the people I love, my family and the older farmers round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using every tool that pays its way and drop the ones that don't. I'd put my savings into renting another eighty hectares next door, because the old boy there wants to retire. And I'd keep pushing the estate to buy a proper autonomous sprayer once one's proven on a farm like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a quieter world suits people you love. Who do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, for one. He's sixty and he still farms the way his dad did, mostly. And our vicar, who's been worried sick about young people losing work. I want progress, but I don't want it to tear up the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rent the eighty hectares even without bigger AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. Good land is good land. Owning or renting more ground has never been a bad idea round here.

S0.say: He'd say AI is still a good tool and the farmers who use it well will stay ahead, urging people not to drop it when the hype fades and posting what's worth paying for on the arable forum.
S0.think: He'd be privately let down, having planned on self-driving tractors, but still ahead of most farmers. He notes a quieter world suits his family and the older farmers he cares about.
S0.do: Keeps tools that pay their way and drops the rest, uses savings to rent another eighty hectares from a retiring neighbour and pushes the estate to buy an autonomous sprayer once proven elsewhere.
S0.quote: I want progress, but I don't want it to tear up the village.
S0.fieldNote: Adam is the eager adopter of this group but anchored by traditional loyalties: his father, the vicar, the village. He sees land as the steady bet whatever happens with AI. His disappointment at the plateau is mild and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'm already betting on, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farming, more food from less ground with less chemical. The farms that adapt will win, and the government should stay out of the way and let farmers choose. I'd say the young ones should learn it, and learn proper farming too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd think I'm in a strong position. I know the tech, I've got land and savings, and the estate trusts me. The risk is the lads on the estate, Jim the tractor driver and the two seasonal lads, because the machines will do their jobs first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the estate to buy two autonomous tractors and train Jim to supervise them, so he's not just let go. I'd expand my own farm by renting more land and buy a small autonomous machine myself. I'd also start an advisory side business, helping other farms set up their kit, maybe a day a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit uneasy about Jim and the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want government to stay out of it. Who looks after Jim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate, first, and the community. I'd make sure he's trained and kept on if I can. That's better than him waiting for a cheque from someone in an office who's never met him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you go too fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I can get carried away. Freya tells me I treat new machines like puppies. She's not wrong.

S1.say: He'd call it good for farming, more food from less ground with fewer chemicals, and say the farms that adapt will win while the government stays out of the way. Young people should learn both the technology and proper farming.
S1.think: He thinks he's in a strong position with skills, land, savings and the estate's trust. His worry is for the tractor driver Jim and the seasonal workers whose jobs machines would take first.
S1.do: Gets the estate to buy two autonomous tractors and trains Jim to supervise them, expands his own farm by renting more land and buying a small autonomous machine, and starts a one-day-a-week advisory business for other farms.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, a little uneasy about Jim and the seasonal workers.
S1.quote: That's better than him waiting for a cheque from someone in an office who's never met him.
S1.fieldNote: Adam sees steady disruption as his moment, but takes personal responsibility for Jim rather than leaving him to the state, which fits his traditional views. His partner Freya gently checks his enthusiasm. He would automate, expand and advise all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. Even I think that's too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the most important thing is keeping families and villages together, and keeping food coming. The government will have to help people, but it should be through work and communities where it can. I'd tell people at church to look out for their neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think a machine that can do anything can also manage the estate better than me. My edge is being early, and in two years there's no early, it's just everyone at once. What I'd still have is land, and that's what I'd hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd put my savings into buying land, maybe the forty hectares next to mine, before prices jump or crash. I'd buy whatever autonomous kit I could afford and farm my own ground with it. And I'd help Jim and the lads find something, through the church and the young farmers, because two years isn't long for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me one chance to grab the right thing, and I'd grab land. With two years you don't learn anything new, you just make one or two big decisions and hope they're right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're buying land and machines while others lose work. How does that sit with your faith?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasily. I'd have to make sure I'm using it for more than me, giving people work where I can, feeding people. Otherwise what was it all for?

S2.say: He'd say keeping families and villages together and food coming matters most, that government help should run through work and communities where possible, and tell people at church to look out for their neighbours.
S2.think: He thinks a machine that can do anything could manage the estate better than him; his edge is being early, and two years means everyone is early at once. Land is what he'd still have.
S2.do: Uses savings to buy land at once, possibly the forty hectares beside his own, buys autonomous machines to farm it himself, and helps the estate workers find other work through the church and the young farmers' club.
S2.feel: Anxious but not frozen, and steadied by being busy.
S2.quote: With two years you don't learn anything new, you just make one or two big decisions and hope they're right.
S2.fieldNote: Even the keenest adopter in this group finds two years too fast and falls back on land as security. Challenged on faith, he admitted unease and reframed his gains as a duty to give work and feed people. His community ties shape how he'd help others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Now that's a race I could run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for farmers to get ready if they start now. I'd tell everyone at the club to learn the machines and buy land if they can. And I'd say the government's main job is to stop red tape slowing people down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think this is the best one for me. Two or three years of running the new kit and helping others set up, and then I'd want to own enough ground to farm with machines and not need the estate job. That's my dream, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd build the advisory side up properly and charge a fair day rate. By year two or three I'd buy or rent another hundred hectares and set it up with my own autonomous kit. I'd also make sure Jim's trained by then, so he can run machines for me or the estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and anxious at the same time, like the start of harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Freya think about putting so much into land and machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd want us to buy a house first, which is fair. We'd probably do both, smaller house, bigger fields. She's a teacher, so she knows what it's like when things change faster than people can learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the village in your five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. If farms need two people instead of twenty, the school shrinks, the shop shuts. I'd want to put some of what I earn back into the village, the hall, the club, the church roof.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough if farmers start now, tell the club to learn the machines and buy land if they can, and say the government's main job is to cut red tape.
S3.think: He thinks this is the best picture for him: a few years running new kit and advising others, then owning enough land to farm with machines and leave the estate job.
S3.do: Builds the advisory business in year one at a fair day rate, buys or rents another hundred hectares with his own autonomous kit by year two or three, and trains Jim so he can run machines for him or the estate.
S3.feel: Excited and anxious at once, like the start of harvest.
S3.quote: If farms need two people instead of twenty, the school shrinks, the shop shuts.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is Adam's ideal timeline, and he sees a clear path to farming his own land with machines. His real worry is the village emptying out, which he'd answer with private giving, not state programmes. Freya's priority on a house pulls his plans towards family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty. I'd be thirty-seven and ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is more than enough for anyone willing to work at it. Learn the tech, keep your land, look after your neighbours. That's what I'd tell the club and my own kids one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd expect to do very well. Ten years of building, buying land and getting the best machines, and by 2036 I'd be farming a lot of ground with very few people. The worry is that I'd be fine and the village wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Freya and buy a house in the first couple of years, then put everything else into land and machines step by step. I'd keep the advisory business going. And I'd help set up something like an apprenticeship with the estate and the club, so young people learn both the machines and the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful, with a worry at the back about the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said by 2036 you'd farm a lot of ground with very few people. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a bit. It's good business and it's bad for the school. I haven't worked out how to square that, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to learn in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to work hard, how to fix things and how to look after people. And how to read a field, even if a drone can do it for them. Some things you should still know with your own eyes.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is more than enough for anyone willing to work: learn the tech, keep your land, look after your neighbours.
S4.think: He expects to do very well, farming a lot of ground with very few people by 2036, but worries he'd be fine while the village wouldn't be.
S4.do: Marries Freya and buys a house in the first couple of years, then puts savings into land and machines step by step. Keeps the advisory business and helps set up an apprenticeship with the estate and the young farmers' club.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, with a lingering worry about the village.
S4.quote: It's good business and it's bad for the school. I haven't worked out how to square that, honestly.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Adam expects to thrive and openly admits a contradiction he can't resolve: efficient farming empties the village. His answer leans on apprenticeships and family values rather than state help. He is the most comfortable of these farmers with every AGI timeline except the fastest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even someone who loves the tech gets one shot at the right decision. What would help is less red tape on buying land and kit, and real support for apprenticeships and village life, run locally, not from an office far away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to villages. Everyone asks about jobs and money, but if farms need hardly anyone, the village dies. I'd want someone thinking about that.

headlineQuote: It's good business and it's bad for the school. I haven't worked out how to square that, honestly.
portrait: Adam Hansen is a 27-year-old farm manager on a grain and oilseed estate who also farms forty hectares he inherited, and he uses AI and drones every day. He's an early adopter with traditional values: free markets, family, church and the village. In the slower pictures he plans to automate, rent more land and start an advisory business while looking after the estate's tractor driver, Jim. In the two-year picture he finds even his speed isn't enough and makes one big bet on land. With five or ten years he expects to thrive, but openly struggles with the fact that farming with very few people could empty his village.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because even an early adopter would get only one chance to make the right decision.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape on buying land and machines, and locally run support for apprenticeships and village life.
